items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The names say what they hold (`jobs`, `errors`, `worker`, `workers`, `pending`). The docstring explains the cancellation and error behaviour, and inline comments cover the less obvious cleanup loop. The only short name, `w`, is a comprehension loop variable.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: It hand-builds structured cancellation: `gather` plus a manual cancel/wait loop (`while True: pending = [...]; await asyncio.wait(pending)`) and an `errors` list, all in one function of about 55 lines. `asyncio.TaskGroup` with a semaphore would do this in a few lines.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It validates `max_concurrent < 1` and keeps task exceptions, but `raise errors[0]` silently drops every later exception. Also, `except asyncio.CancelledError: pass` in the cleanup loop ignores repeated cancellations, so a task with a hanging cleanup could leave run_tasks impossible to cancel.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: An empty list returns at once (`if not workers: return`), and `max_concurrent < 1` raises ValueError. But when a task raises, the other tasks are not cancelled and queued tasks still start ("the remaining tasks still run"). Only the first exception is re-raised at the end. The behaviour is documented and nothing leaks.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: `async def run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None` matches the spec. Workers call `job()` lazily, only when a slot is free. It uses only the standard library and nothing runs at import time.
